To support these plantations, they imported laborers from China and Melanesia. Therefore, China was one of the countries that sent many workers to Samoa for cocoa and rubber plantations.

The term for different documents that represent the same original text is "witnesses." In textual criticism, these witnesses undergo comparison to identify variant readings, which are differences between the versions. The goal of textual criticism is to determine the most authentic version of the original text by examining how each variant may have been introduced, whether through accidental or intentional means. The result is a critical text, or critical edition, that strives to best approximate the original. This critical text should also document variant readings to show the relationship between the existing witnesses and the reconstructed original. Textual critics consider both external evidence, such as the age, provenance, and affiliation of each witness, and internal or physical considerations, like the author's and scribes' or printers' likely actions, when establishing the critical text.

The title of CBC's flagship newscast is "The National." It airs Sunday through Friday at 10:00 p.m. EST and Saturdays at 6:00 p.m. EST. Before October 2006, CBC's owned-and-operated stations aired a second broadcast of the program at 11:00 p.m., which excluded the analysis and documentary segment. Queen Victoria blamed Prime Minister William E. Gladstone for the death of General Charles George Gordon at Khartoum in 1885. Gordon was killed during the Siege of Khartoum, which occurred when Gladstone's government had ordered the evacuation of the city but was unable to carry out the operation in time to save Gordon and his troops. This event was a low point in Gladstone's third term as prime minister, and Victoria's criticism was reflective of the widespread discontent with his government's handling of the situation.

The terms "morphology-based" and "appearance-based" refer to a traditional approach in systematics, the classification of organisms based on their physical characteristics. This approach has often been used to classify hexapods, a group that includes insects, springtails, Protura, and Diplura. These four groups were traditionally classified together as Hexapoda, with insects forming one group and the other three being grouped together as Entognatha due to their internalized mouthparts. However, recent studies based on evolutionary history and genetic data suggest that Hexapoda may be polyphyletic, meaning that the last common ancestor of the group was not a member of Hexapoda. Many of the traditional appearance-based taxa have been shown to be paraphyletic, which means that they do not include all the descendants of their last common ancestor. Therefore, it is now considered better to use monophyletic groupings, where the last common ancestor is a member of the group, for the classification of insects.

The FA Cup victory in 1901 was won by Tottenham Hotspur, who defeated Sheffield United. Marshal Murat led 120,000 troops into Spain in early 1808, as part of Napoleon's plans to mediate between rival political factions in the country. Based on historical records, a significant portion of Bermuda's black population can trace some aspect of their ancestry back to Native Americans. This is most notably the case with St David's Islanders, although many who have such ancestry are often unaware of it. During the colonial period, large-scale deportations occurred, with hundreds of Native Americans, including Algonquian peoples displaced from southern New England colonies, being shipped to Bermuda. This influx was particularly noticeable following the Pequot and King Philip's Wars in the 17th century, when many Native Americans were sold into slavery.

A USB host can implement more than one host controller, according to the USB (Universal Serial Bus) design architecture. These host controllers can provide one or more USB ports, allowing for multiple peripheral devices to be connected in a tiered-star topology. This topology can branch into a tree structure with up to five tier levels, including additional USB hubs. Each host controller can support up to 127 devices, including hub devices, if present.

Yes, the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations (RICO) Act is still in use today. Initiated in response to organized crime, the FBI began investigating and dismantling former Prohibition-organized groups that had become fronts for crime in various cities and towns, using the provisions provided in the RICO Act. The FBI's Top Hoodlum Program was created to gather information on mobsters and report it regularly to a centralized collection of intelligence on racketeers. After the RICO Act took effect, the FBI started conducting undercover operations against known organized crime syndicates and families, leading to the dismantling of many of these groups. The RICO Act remains a crucial tool for addressing organized crime and any individuals who may fall under its purview even today.

Salafis and Zahiris are two groups of Muslims who advocate for Quranic literalism, which is the belief that the Quran should be interpreted strictly according to its literal or apparent meaning. Salafis and Zahiris reject the idea of engaging in esoteric or metaphorical interpretations of the Quran, and instead insist on a literal reading of the text. This approach to interpreting the Quran is in contrast to other scholars and commentators who believe that the Quran has hidden or inner meanings that can only be understood through esoteric or mystical interpretation.

Distinguishing small differences in color is challenging for both human vision and video compression algorithms. When compressing video data, these algorithms take advantage of the fact that small color differences are harder to perceive than changes in brightness. By averaging a color across similar areas, they can reduce the storage space required, similar to JPEG image compression. This is why it can be hard to tell smaller differences involved, especially in the color domain, when dealing with compressed video data.

Harper Lee, the author of "To Kill a Mockingbird," started refusing interviews and questions about the book in 1964. Initially, she welcomed the attention and fame that came with the novel's success, participating in interviews, visiting schools, and attending events that honored the book. However, as the years passed, she became increasingly uncomfortable with the repetitive nature of the questions and the celebrity-like attention she received. In 1995, she wrote a letter declining to provide an introduction for a special edition of the book, stating that introductions inhibit pleasure and kill the joy of anticipation. She believed that "Mockingbird still says what it has to say" and has managed to survive the years without the need for preamble.

General Sir Henry Clinton attempted to seize Charles Town (present-day Charleston, South Carolina) during the American Revolution. In June 1776, Clinton, leading 2,000 men and a naval squadron, aimed to capture the city, expecting a simultaneous Loyalist uprising in the region. However, the attempt was unsuccessful. The unfinished yet sturdy palmetto-log walls of Fort Sullivan withstood the British cannonballs. Moreover, local Loyalists did not join the attack as anticipated. Instead, Colonel William Moultrie's American forces returned fire, causing significant damage to several British ships. As a result, the British were compelled to retreat, and the fort was later renamed Fort Moultrie to honor its commander.

The Bayfront Park Amphitheater in Miami is notable for hosting outdoor music events. Jim Foster worked for the Chicago Blitz, which was a team in the United States Football League (USFL). Foster, who was previously involved in the NFL, joined the USFL in 1982 and became the executive vice-president of the Chicago Blitz. It was while working for the Blitz that Foster began developing his concept of arena football, using his spare time to organize a test game. The USFL eventually ceased operations in 1985, allowing Foster to focus solely on arena football. The test game for his new concept was eventually held on April 27, 1986.

Hydrogen poses several threats to human safety. Its high flammability and tendency to mix with air make it susceptible to explosive detonations and fires. Moreover, in its pure, oxygen-free form, hydrogen can act as an asphyxiant, posing a risk of suffocation. Additionally, liquid hydrogen is a cryogen and can cause frostbite due to its extremely low temperature. Hydrogen can also dissolve in certain metals, causing adverse effects like hydrogen embrittlement, which can lead to cracks and explosions. Hydrogen gas leaks can spontaneously ignite when they come into contact with external air, and hydrogen fires are almost invisible, increasing the risk of accidental burns.
Mary is called Maryam in Islam. She holds a revered position in the Quran, with an entire chapter dedicated to her, and is also described as the mother of Jesus.

The statement "The world will never again see five million people crying together" was made by Sherif Hetata, a former political prisoner and member of Nasser's Arab Socialist Union (ASU). This observation was a reflection on the outpouring of nationalistic passion and grief seen after the death of Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser. With millions of people mourning and taking to the streets across Arab cities, it was a testament to Nasser's profound impact and influence on the Arab world during his time as a leader.

In order to hunt protected species, a hunting license is universally required across all states. This license may necessitate the completion of a hunting safety course prior to its acquisition. The term "Near and Middle East" came into use a few years before the start of World War I. This terminology, however, did not gain wide acceptance, particularly from a colonial perspective that viewed the entire region as a single entity. A notable example can be found in the account of Captain T.C. Fowle, 40th Pathans (troops of British India), who undertook a journey from Karachi to Syria just prior to the war. In his book, published before the war, the term "Near East" is absent, and the entire region is referred to as "the Middle East." The areas that were once considered part of the "Near East" are now identified as "Turkish" territories, rather than Ottoman.

The use of Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) as a standard tool of diagnosis is currently hindered by its cost and application. Although PCR technology has the capability to detect any infectious agent rapidly and specifically, its application is not beneficial for the diagnosis of certain diseases such as tetanus and botulism. These clostridial diseases are caused by a small number of infectious bacteria that produce highly potent neurotoxins, and since a significant proliferation of the infectious agent does not occur, the ability of PCR to detect the presence of these bacteria is limited. However, it is worth noting that the cost and application challenges in PCR are not insurmountable, and ongoing advancements in technology are expected to address these issues.

Toxocara canis infections are spread through the ingestion of eggs present in dog feces. These eggs can cause toxocariasis, a disease that affects approximately 14% of the population in the United States and 24% in Great Britain, with around 10,000 cases reported annually in the US. If left untreated, toxocariasis can lead to retinal damage and decreased vision.

The approved algorithms for MPEG-1 Audio Layer I, II, and III were finalized in 1992, as part of the MPEG-1 standard suite, which was published as the international standard ISO/IEC 11172-3 (also known as MPEG-1 Audio or MPEG-1 Part 3) in 1993.

Chopin preferred to play his compositions in intimate settings, such as his own Paris apartment, where he would perform for small groups of friends. While he did give the occasional public performance at the Salle Pleyel, he was known for acquiring a reputation of the highest order based on a minimum of public appearances. In fact, there are few more than thirty documented public performances throughout his lifetime. Chopin's preference for private performances allowed him to create a more personal and intimate connection with his listeners, making his apartment the ideal venue for showcasing his unique pianistic skills and expressive compositions.

The Congress of Erfurt was held in the year 1808. This meeting was significant as it was held before Napoleon's campaign in Iberia and was aimed at addressing lingering issues with the Russians. Napoleon sought to keep Russia on his side during the upcoming struggle in Spain and in any potential conflict against Austria. The agreement reached at this congress, the Erfurt Convention, included provisions such as calling for Britain to cease its war against France, recognizing the Russian conquest of Finland from Sweden, and affirming Russian support for France in a possible war against Austria.

The French had planned to transport their troops to Britain for the invasion in 1759 by utilizing their Brest and Toulon fleets. The troops were to be gathered near the mouth of the Loire. However, this invasion never came to fruition due to two significant naval defeats. In August, the French Mediterranean fleet, led by Jean-François de La Clue-Sabran, was defeated by a larger British fleet under Edward Boscawen at the Battle of Lagos. Then, in the Battle of Quiberon Bay on 20 November, the British admiral Edward Hawke, with 23 ships of the line, defeated the French Brest fleet of 21 ships of the line under Marshal de Conflans. The British forces sank, captured, or forced many of the French ships aground, effectively ending the French plans for an invasion of Britain.

The shipping expeditions of the Dutch East India Company (VOC) and the Dutch West India Company (WIC) were primarily overseen by the States General of the United Provinces. However, many of these expeditions were initially driven by the maritime interests of individual provinces. In particular, Holland and Zeeland played a significant role in launching these ventures. As coastal provinces with strong maritime traditions, Holland and Zeeland had the resources, expertise, and motivation to invest in shipping and exploration, making them key contributors to the Dutch era of exploration and trade.

Madonna became involved with personal trainer Carlos Leon around the time she released her sixth studio album, Bedtime Stories, in 1994. The concealment of multiracial heritage in the United States was prevalent until the mid-20th century. This was primarily due to the racial discrimination faced by minorities, which led many people of mixed ancestry to identify or be classified as belonging to only one ethnicity, often that of the culture in which they were raised. The social and cultural identities, rather than DNA, play a significant role in how individuals perceive themselves. However, with the progression of time and the erosion of racial discrimination, people have become more open to acknowledging and expressing their multiracial heritage.

The Jews were described as enemies of Christ by Pope St. Gregory in his writings. He stigmatized Judaism and the Jewish people, and strongly expressed his view that as the Holy Spirit's influence expanded throughout the world, the hatred of the Jews only grew more intense. He further accused Judaism of being a source of pollution and deception, and labeled all heresy as "Jewish." The poet Rumi passed away in the year 1273. He is known for his significant contribution to mystical poetry, particularly in his book Mathnawi where he frequently references and interprets the Quran. Rumi's work is recognized for its heavy use of Quranic passages, making it a valuable resource for those seeking a Sufi interpretation of the holy text.

In the 21st century, online webcomics have emerged as a prominent type of comic. This form of comics is expressed through images, often accompanied by text or other visual information, and published on the internet. Webcomics can take various structures, including sequential panels with textual devices such as speech balloons and captions, and can use cartooning, illustration, or even photographic images. Every Roman legionary camp included religious personnel as part of its organization, with a hierarchy of religious officials, standard bearers, and assistants, as well as shrines for various gods and deities. The religious practices in the camps were diverse, encompassing the worship of traditional Roman gods like Jupiter, as well as personal deities and household gods. From the early Imperial era, soldiers also gave cult to the emperor and his family, and by the Severan era, they offered cult to the Imperial divi, the current emperor's numen, genius, and domus, and even to the Empress as "mother of the camp." The later Imperial era saw the emergence of legionary shrines to Mithras, which were not part of official cult until Mithras was absorbed into Solar and Stoic Monism as a focus of military concordia and Imperial loyalty.

The earliest confirmed evidence of the Chinese script is found on oracle bones, which are inscriptions on bones and turtle shells from the late Shang dynasty (circa 1200-1050 BC). These artifacts, which were initially sold as "dragon bones" for medicinal purposes, were identified as Chinese writing by scholars in 1899. The bones were traced back to a village near Anyang in Henan Province, where excavations conducted by the Academia Sinica between 1928 and 1937 uncovered over 150,000 fragments.

Indigenous peoples in Arctic zones use fur for warmth and protection. The use of fur in this region is rooted in prehistoric times and continues to be valued for its thermal properties and durability. Despite being a subject of controversy in developed countries due to concerns over animal cruelty, fur remains a crucial resource for indigenous communities in the Arctic, where the harsh climate necessitates warm and protective clothing.

The Necessary, in Avicenna's metaphysics, is detached from time. This means that the Necessary Existent due-to-Itself is not subject to the constraints of time, and its existence is not dependent on or influenced by temporal phenomena. The Necessary exists 'due-to-Itself' and has no quiddity/essence other than existence. It is one, indivisible, and unchanging, and does not possess any of the characteristics of temporal existence, such as genus, definition, counterpart, opposite, matter, quality, quantity, place, situation, or time.

The peace talks between India and Pakistan became serious in the year 2004. This development was significant given the history of conflicts between the two nations, including major battles in Punjab in the wars of 1965 and 1971. Punjab is also home to key sites of Pakistan's nuclear program and major military bases, making the peace process all the more crucial. The peace process has helped to reduce tensions, enabling the increase of trade and people-to-people contacts through the Wagah border. Additionally, Indian Sikh pilgrims are now able to visit holy sites in Pakistan, such as Nankana Sahib.

The materials from the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) collection are located in the Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A). The V&A, in collaboration with RIBA, features some items from the RIBA collections in the V&A + RIBA Architecture Gallery, as well as in temporary exhibitions across Europe and North America. The RIBA Library, also known as the British Architectural Library, was established in 1834 and is one of the three largest architectural libraries in the world, with over four million items, the largest in Europe.

Deep Ecology is a philosophical and ethical movement that emerged in the 1970s, focusing on the inherent worth of non-human life and the interconnectedness of all living things. It goes beyond traditional environmentalism, advocating for a radical rethinking of human relationship with nature, and promoting a shift towards a more sustainable and equitable balance between human needs and the health of the planet. Deep Ecology emphasizes the importance of biodiversity, wilderness preservation, and respect for the intrinsic value of all living beings, encouraging a profound appreciation and understanding of the complex web of life.

The Western part of the Umayyad Caliphate's empire gained its independence under the leadership of Abd-ar-Rahman I. Following the collapse of the Umayyad Caliphate in 750, the western part of the empire, including the region that is now Portugal, became independent and established the Emirate of Córdoba.

The original ancestors of the Tibetan people are represented by the six red bands in the Tibetan flag, which symbolize the Se, Mu, Dong, Tong, Dru, and Ra ethnic groups. These groups are considered the historical forebears of the Tibetan population.

The first station launched after the original BBC was ITV. The launch of BBC2, which was renamed from BBC TV in 1964, was preceded by the introduction of ITV, the second television station in the UK. BBC2 was launched to provide more niche programming and was the first British channel to use UHF and 625-line pictures, offering higher definition than the existing VHF 405-line system.

The test game in the inaugural season of the International Hockey League (IHL) featured two teams: the Rockford Metros and the Chicago Politicians. In addition, fossils from recent geological periods resemble species still living in the same area, as observed by Darwin in South America and William Clift in Australia.

Hunters strongly felt that Internet hunting, which involves hunting over the Internet using remotely controlled guns, violated the principles of fair chase. Fair chase is a fundamental element of hunting tradition, emphasizing the importance of being in the field with one's firearm or bow. According to a representative from the National Rifle Association (NRA), Internet hunting, which is primarily done through desktop computers by clicking a mouse, is not consistent with the values and practices of hunting.

The written form of Tibetan is based on Classical Tibetan, which provides a consistent written standard amidst the regional variations in spoken Tibetan. This consistency can be traced back to the influence of the Tibetan empire, whose rule extended across a large part of the Tibetan linguistic area, encompassing regions from northern Pakistan in the west to Yunnan and Sichuan in the east, and as far south as Bhutan. The Tibetan language has its own script, which it shares with Ladakhi and Dzongkha, and which is derived from the ancient Indian Brāhmī script.

The term "Hokkien" is commonly used in Southeast Asia to refer to a group of Chinese dialects, specifically those that belong to the Min Nan branch of Chinese linguistics. These dialects are also known as Southern Min and are classified under the Quanzhang Division, which is named after the first characters of the two main Hokkien urban centers, Quanzhou and Zhangzhou. The term "Hokkien" itself simply means "Fujian province" in Chinese, reflecting the origins of these dialects in the Fujian region of China.
Gateway Community College was previously located in the Long Wharf district of New Haven before it moved to its current campus in the downtown area.

The Playstation 3, in its initial years, faced challenges in gaining market share due to its high cost and a limited selection of high-quality games. This put it at a disadvantage compared to its predecessor, the Playstation 2, and its competitors, such as the Xbox 360 and the Nintendo Wii. The Xbox 360, although not the best-selling console of the seventh generation, was still considered a success as it helped Microsoft establish itself as a major player in the console market. The Nintendo Wii, despite selling the most console units, experienced a decline in third-party software support in its later years. The Playstation 3's sales and game titles improved significantly in its later years, but it took some time for it to reach parity with the Xbox 360.

The peace agreement was renamed "Magna Carta." This name was given to the charter that resulted from the meeting between King John and the rebel leaders at Runnymede, near Windsor Castle, on 15 June 1215. The charter was initially created as a proposal for political reform, focusing on the rights of free men, not serfs and unfree labor. It included provisions for the protection of church rights, protection from illegal imprisonment, access to swift justice, new taxation only with baronial consent, and limitations on scutage and other feudal payments. Additionally, a council of twenty-five barons was established to monitor and ensure the king's adherence to the charter.

The largest Carnival celebration is held in the city of Panjim, which is the capital of the Indian state of Goa. This Roman Catholic tradition, known as Intruz in Goa, was introduced by the Portuguese who ruled Goa for over four centuries and is celebrated annually before the Christian season of Lent. The celebration in Panjim is the most significant one in the state, featuring all-night parades with bands, dances, and floats, as well as grand balls in the evenings. The European tradition of Fat Tuesday is also observed, with the eating of crepes or "AleBelle" filled with freshly grated coconut and jaggery. The festivities last for three days and nights, peaking on the Tuesday preceding Ash Wednesday, when the legendary King Momo takes over the state.

Frédéric Chopin, the renowned Polish composer and pianist, gave approximately 30 public performances during the last 18 years of his life. Chopin, who settled in Paris at the age of 21, was known to prefer the intimate atmosphere of salons over public concerts. He earned his living by selling compositions and teaching piano to students, who held him in high regard. Despite his limited public appearances, Chopin was highly admired by many of his musical contemporaries, including Franz Liszt and Robert Schumann. His final years were marked by financial support from his admirer Jane Stirling, who also facilitated his visit to Scotland in 1848. Chopin's life was marked by poor health, and he passed away in Paris in 1849, likely due to tuberculosis.

The term for the class of insects that are wingless is Apterygota. This group consists of primitive wingless insects, including the order of silverfish (Thysanura). It's worth noting that the classification of Thysanura is debated, with some evidence suggesting that it may not be monophyletic. Nonetheless, Apterygota stands as a significant category of insects that lack wings.

Based on available data as of 2012, renewable energy sources, such as solar, wind, and hydroelectric power, are responsible for around half of all new electrical capacity added. This significant milestone indicates the growing competitiveness and importance of renewable energy in the global energy landscape.

Jaipur, also known as the "Pink City," is renowned for its distinctive houses made from a type of sandstone that has a dominant pink hue. This sandstone gives the city a unique and cohesive appearance, setting it apart from other cities in Rajasthan.

The astronomical observatory with a 7.3-meter-long aerial telescope, set up by Edmond Halley in 1676 in Saint Helena, is located in the Longwood district, near Saint Mathew's Church in Hutt's Gate. The site is now known as Halley's Mount, which stands 680 meters (2,230 feet) high and is named after the esteemed astronomer.

The primary religion of East and South Slavic populations is Orthodox Christianity. This Christian denomination was introduced to the pagan Slavic communities during the 6th to 10th centuries, and it continues to be the dominant faith in these regions. The religious divide between the East and West Slavs is largely consistent with the East-West Schism that originated in the 11th century. Nowadays, the majority of religious Slavs are Orthodox, while a significant minority are Roman Catholic. A small portion of Slavs practices Protestantism or Islam, and there is also a minority who identify as atheist or agnostic.

Enki was the chief god of Eridu, a city that was established at the beginning of the Ubaid period, around 5300 BC, and remained an important religious center throughout its history. Eridu was the first settlement established in southern Mesopotamia by farmers who brought with them the Hadji Muhammed culture, which pioneered irrigation agriculture. The city was a religious center even as it was surpassed in size by the nearby city of Uruk. The story of the passing of the me, or gifts of civilization, from Enki to Inanna, the goddess of Uruk, reflects the shift in hegemony from Eridu to Uruk. As the chief god of Eridu, Enki was a central figure in the religious and cultural life of the city.

Six men were in the top twelve during season five of American Idol. This was due to the show's format at the time, which divided the twenty-four semi-finalists by gender to ensure equal representation in the top twelve. The men and women performed separately in the semi-finals, with the bottom two from each group eliminated each week. This continued until only six men and six women remained, forming the top twelve for the season.

Carly Smithson, a contestant on American Idol's seventh season, received significant attention due to her prior recording contract. She was one of several contestants that season who had previously worked in the music industry, leading to the media dubbing them "the ringers." Smithson's professional experience distinguished her from the other contestants and made her a subject of interest during the season.

The Proclamation of 1763, issued by George III, prohibited white settlement beyond the Appalachian mountains to appease American Indian tribes. However, this decree led to significant outrage in the Thirteen Colonies, as its inhabitants were eager to acquire native lands for settlement. This dissatisfaction contributed to the growing unrest between the American colonies and the British government, which ultimately led to the American Revolution.

The person whose name includes a Christian rite of passage from the Bible was viewed as "holier than all men born of woman" by some theologians in the Byzantine East. This view is particularly associated with Gregory Nazianzen's Mariology and was developed by later theologians such as Sophronius of Jerusalem and John Damascene. According to Sophronius, Mary was already immaculate when she was "purified" at the Annunciation, making John the Baptist, who was sanctified in utero, "holier than all men born of woman." John Damascene further honored Mary by stating that she "purified the waters of baptism by touching them," a privilege previously attributed to Christ. This view of Mary's absolute holiness and unsullied human nature is based on her "pre-purification" and is attributed to the Damascene's influence. This theological perspective regards Mary as being of surpassing holiness, even greater than John the Baptist and equal to Christ in purity.

The prefix "prě-", meaning "trans-" or "over-", developed into "prije-" in western Ijekavian dialects and some Ikavian dialects, instead of the expected "pre-". This change occurred due to the potential for ambiguity with the prefix "pri-", which has different meanings such as "approach" or "come close to". By changing to "prije-", the two prefixes were distinguished more clearly and avoided confusion in these dialects.

The United States declared war for the first time in its history upon the United Kingdom, in 1812. The conflict, known as the War of 1812, was primarily due to Britain's policy of blocking American shipments to France, which was then at war with Britain. This policy affected the United States' pursuit of overseas trade, a significant aspect of its economy. Additionally, Britain impressed American seamen into the Royal Navy and supported an Indian insurrection in the American Midwest, aiming to create an Indian state that would hinder American expansion. These actions led to the U.S. declaring war on the United Kingdom, marking the first time it had officially engaged in a war.

The New Orleans Hornets, now known as the Pelicans, temporarily relocated to Oklahoma City in 2005 due to the devastation caused by Hurricane Katrina. They played their home games at the Ford Center, now named Chesapeake Energy Arena, for two seasons before returning to New Orleans. This makes the Hornets the first major league sports franchise to be based in Oklahoma, if only temporarily.

The Compass-M1 satellite shares a similar purpose with the GIOVE satellites, both serving to test and validate signals and file frequencies for their respective systems, Compass and Galileo. These experimental satellites play a crucial role in the initial development and implementation of global navigation satellite systems.

The general temperature of a coastal location during the night in the European Mediterranean region is typically between 6-8 °C (43-46 °F). This estimate is based on the temperature range in various coastal locations in Cyprus, including Limassol, during the winter and early spring months of January to March.

The rota system was an unconventional power succession system in which power was transferred to the eldest member of the ruling dynasty, rather than from father to son. This system was prone to creating conflict and rivalry within the royal family, as power was not guaranteed to go to the immediate next of kin. The system was particularly contentious during the time of the Yaroslavichi rule, when the established rotation was bypassed in the establishment of Vladimir II Monomakh as the Grand Prince of Kiev. This decision led to significant power struggles between various branches of the family, including the Olegovichi from Chernihiv, the Monomakhs from Pereyaslav, the Izyaslavichi from Turov/Volhynia, and the Polotsk Princes.

Orthodox scholars often refer to the Ecumenical Councils when defending their approach to interpreting canonical rules. The canons, as compiled in the Pēdálion, are considered foundational guidelines in the Orthodox tradition, with bishops adapting them to local circumstances. The use of the term "kanónes/κανόνες" (rules) instead of "nómoi/νόμοι" (laws) by the Greek-speaking Ecumenical Councils suggests a flexible interpretation. However, the dogmatic decisions of these councils are regarded as essential and are to be followed strictly to maintain the Church's unity.

Small social groups can enforce morality through social forces such as gossip and reputation. When groups become larger, it becomes more difficult to enforce morality through these means. Therefore, humans may have created gods and spirits as a way to extend the social enforcement of morality to these larger groups. This strategy allows for the restraint of selfishness and the promotion of cooperation within the group.

Italian Summer feasts are held in the North End of the city. These feasts are annual events that honor Catholic saints and are a significant part of the city's cultural heritage. The North End is a historic neighborhood in the city, known for its strong Italian-American community and influence.

The early Puritan movement aimed to reform the Church of England to resemble the Protestant churches of Europe, particularly those in Geneva. This desire for reformation was driven by the success of the Counter-Reformation on the Continent and the growth of a Puritan party dedicated to further Protestant reform.

The Second Council of Nicea, also known as the seventh ecumenical council, took place in the year 787. This council reaffirmed the use of religious images or icons in Christian worship, which had been practiced since the early church. The veneration of icons, including those of Mary, is based on the understanding that those who venerate the image are venerating the reality of the person it represents. This practice is followed by both the Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christian traditions.

Lok-Ham Chan, a distinguished professor of history at the University of Washington, has conducted extensive research on Changchub Gyaltsen, the founder of the Phagmodrupa Dynasty in Tibet. According to Chan, Changchub Gyaltsen was a nationalist who aimed to recreate the old Tibetan Kingdom that existed during the Chinese Tang dynasty, build "nationalist sentiment" amongst Tibetans, and remove all traces of Mongol suzerainty. Chan also notes that Changchub Gyaltsen adopted the old administrative system of Songtsän Gampo, the first leader of the Tibetan Empire, by reinstating its legal code of punishments and administrative units. This included dividing Central Tibet into districts with district heads who had to conform to old rituals and wear clothing styles of old Imperial Tibet. Therefore, it is clear that Lok-Ham Chan's academic work has been closely associated with the University of Washington.

A measurement of billions of instructions per second in the context of computing is referred to as gigaflops. This unit is used to quantify the computational power of a system, with a typical modern computer being capable of executing operations at this scale. It is not uncommon for such systems to function without errors over extended periods, even when managing large programs comprising multiple million instructions. These programs, which can take years to develop and often contain errors due to their complexity, are used in various applications, such as word processors and web browsers.

Mutaguchi's troops, particularly those at Kohima, suffered from starvation as Japan's supply arrangements were unable to maintain her forces. The lack of supplies became critical once Mutaguchi's hopes for an early victory were dashed. The Allied forces took advantage of the situation and advanced southwards from Kohima and northwards from Imphal, meeting on 22 June and breaking the Japanese siege of Imphal. The Japanese operation was abandoned on 3 July, with over 50,000 troops lost, mostly due to starvation and disease. This marked the Japanese Army's worst defeat up to that point.

Lossless data compression algorithms typically exploit statistical redundancy in data to reduce its size without losing any information. This is achieved by representing data in a way that takes advantage of patterns or repetitions in the data. For instance, in an image, if there are areas of consistent color over several pixels, the data can be encoded as " n consecutive red pixels" instead of "red pixel, red pixel,...". This basic example demonstrates run-length encoding, one of many techniques used to reduce file size by eliminating redundancy. Statistical redundancy is a common characteristic in most real-world data, enabling lossless compression to be possible.

The "hot AC" format remains a viable option in the Adult Contemporary (AC) radio landscape. This format distinguishes itself by incorporating a mix of current and recent hits, often leaning towards a more up-tempo and chart-based selection compared to traditional AC stations. The viability of "hot AC" is particularly noteworthy when considering the challenges faced by other AC formats during the 2005-2007 economic downturn and recession. At that time, many stations shifted towards more chart-based and popular formats, such as CHR, top 40, urban, and Latino, due to the decline in physical record sales affecting the AC genre as a whole.

In 2014, contributions to the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) from governments and the private sector surpassed $1 billion. This significant amount consisted of $477 million allocated to the organization's core resources and an additional $529 million earmarked for particular programs and initiatives.

The Ottoman Empire was founded in 1299 by the leader Osman I, who belonged to the Oghuz Turks. This information comes from historical records that detail the establishment of this empire in northwestern Anatolia. The Oghuz Turks were the founding group of the Ottoman Empire.

In 2013, Bloomberg named Namibia the top emerging market economy in Africa and the 13th best in the world. The ranking was based on various factors including financial-market statistics, IMF forecasts, and World Bank data. Namibia was rated ahead of other African countries such as Morocco, South Africa, and Zambia, and even outperformed countries like Hungary, Brazil, and Mexico. The rankings took into account areas of particular interest to foreign investors, such as the ease of doing business, perceived level of corruption, and economic freedom. To attract foreign investment, the Namibian government has made efforts to reduce red tape and improve business regulations. However, challenges such as cumbersome customs procedures and demands for facilitation payments still exist. Nevertheless, Namibia's standing as an Upper Middle Income country by the World Bank and its ranking of 87th out of 185 economies in terms of ease of doing business, highlights its potential as a favorable destination for investment.

The impeachment process against Hastings was formally called the "Article of Charge of High Crimes and Misdemeanors." This legal procedure was initiated by Burke on April 4, 1786, and it marked a significant event in English history as the first major public discourse on imperialism. Burke's impassioned speech against Hastings, whom he accused of corruption and tyranny, helped to shape public perception of the trial's importance. The charges against Hastings were serious, with Burke describing him as a "captain-general of iniquity" and a "ravenous vulture devouring the carcasses of the dead." Despite the House of Commons' impeachment of Hastings, the House of Lords later acquitted him of all charges.

The overvaluation of bundled subprime mortgages was primarily based on the theory that housing prices would continue to rise or "escalate." This assumption was one of the factors leading to the financial crisis of 2008, as the housing bubble burst and the values of securities tied to U.S. real estate plummeted. The crisis had a global impact, affecting financial institutions, stock markets, and economies worldwide.

In March 2006, smoking was banned in all enclosed public places in Scotland. This law was introduced to improve public health and reduce exposure to secondhand smoke. The ban had a mixed impact on pub sales, with some experiencing a decline while others reported growth in food sales. The Wetherspoon pub chain even reported profits at the top end of expectations two years after the ban. However, some companies like Scottish & Newcastle reported falling sales and attributed their weakness partly to the smoking ban.

The first two countries to recognize the State of Israel were the United States and the Soviet Union. The United States has had a close relationship with Israel, which is considered to be the country's "most reliable partner in the Middle East" due to shared democratic values, religious affinities, and security interests. The two nations have a multidimensional relationship, and the United States has played a leading role in the Arab-Israeli peace process. However, the United States and Israel have differing views on certain issues, such as the Golan Heights, Jerusalem, and settlements. Since 1967, the United States has provided more military assistance and grants to Israel than any other country, with a total of $100 billion provided up until 2003.

The monarchy of Spain, specifically King Alfonso VIII of Castile, requested that Dominic travel to Denmark in 1203. The purpose of this journey was to arrange the marriage between the king's son and a niece of King Valdemar II of Denmark. This information is derived from the account of Dominic's life and travels, which included his participation in the embassy to Denmark as part of his religious and reforming mission.

Canadian media scholar Harold Innis theorized that the type of media people use in communication shapes the structure and durability of society in different ways. He gave the example of ancient Egypt, where they used two types of media: papyrus, which he referred to as "Space Binding," and stone, which he termed "Time Binding." Papyrus, as a space-binding medium, enabled the transmission of written orders across vast distances, facilitating the waging of distant military campaigns and colonial administration. In contrast, stone as a time-binding medium, through the construction of temples and pyramids, sustained the authority of successive generations and allowed for the shaping of communication in their society over time. Innis's work highlights the importance of media in shaping society and its enduring impact on communication.

North Zhejiang and south Jiangsu are renowned for their prosperity and dreaminess, as evidenced by the practice of including place names from these regions, such as Hangzhou and Jiaxing, in poetry to convey a sense of opulence. The cities of Hangzhou and Suzhou, in particular, are so famous for their prosperity that they are the subject of the popular saying "Above there is heaven; below there is Suzhou and Hangzhou." This saying is still a source of pride for the people of these cities, indicating that their reputation for wealth and success continues to this day.

According to a tradition in Islam, as described by George Sale in 1734, every individual, upon birth, is touched by the devil, with the exception of Mary and her firstborn child, Jesus. This tradition suggests that Mary and Jesus were protected from this contact with the evil spirit, and therefore, they are considered to be free from sin, similar to other children of Adam.

The play adaptation of To Kill a Mockingbird, written by Christopher Sergel, was first performed in 1990. The play made its debut in Monroeville, Alabama, which is known as "The Literary Capital of Alabama." The annual performance is a significant event in the town, with local townspeople participating as cast members and even selecting white male audience members to serve on the jury during the courtroom scene. The production is so intertwined with the town's identity that author Albert Murray described it as having a "religious underpinning" and being a part of the town's "civic education."

A low-gain antenna would be the best option when placement is tricky. Unlike high-gain antennas, which require careful aiming and are more sensitive to placement due to their longer range and better signal quality, low-gain antennas have a shorter range and their orientation is relatively unimportant. This makes them more forgiving in terms of placement and ideal for situations where precise aiming is difficult. Examples of low-gain antennas include whip antennas, such as those found on portable radios and cordless phones.

Based on the information provided, the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) has cooperative initiatives with the University of Maryland, which is conveniently located near NARA's secondary facility, Archives II, in College Park, Maryland.
New Delhi is the municipality that serves as the capital of India. It is not only the seat of the Government of India but also the capital of the Delhi territory.

Jewish cultural expressions can differ significantly among various Jewish communities due to the influence of local environments during the Jewish diaspora. One notable way they differ is in culinary preferences. Over the centuries, Jewish communities established in various parts of the Old World developed unique cuisines based on the availability of local ingredients and culinary traditions, resulting in a diverse range of Jewish culinary practices and dishes across communities.

Czech verbs have three grammatical moods: indicative, imperative, and conditional. The indicative mood is used to express facts or statements. The imperative mood is used to give commands or instructions, and it has specific endings for each of the three person (or number) categories. The conditional mood is used to express possible events, and it is formed with a particle after the past-tense verb. This mood is equivalent to the English constructions "I would" or "I wish."

The Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA), founded in 1837, is a professional organization that aims to advance architecture. This goal is reflected in its charter and has been a constant pursuit for over 180 years. RIBA's mission is to promote excellence in architecture, support the architectural profession, and provide guidance on architectural issues to the public, government, and other stakeholders.

Darwin discovered that recently extinct species were more similar to living species than those from earlier eras. This observation supports his theory of common descent and branching evolution through natural selection. Darwin believed that species change gradually over time, but not at the same rate. Some organisms, like Lingula, remain unchanged since the earliest fossils. The pace of natural selection depends on variability and change in the environment, which differentiates his theory from Lamarckian laws of inevitable progress. This concept also anticipates the punctuated equilibrium hypothesis, where evolutionary change occurs in bursts. Furthermore, Darwin noted that patterns of extinction align with his theory, as related groups of species have a continued existence until extinction, and then do not reappear. Fossils from recent geological periods also resemble species still living in the same area, further emphasizing the connection between living and extinct species.

Liu Bei, a Chinese figure from the Three Kingdoms period, was impressed by Nanjing's geographic position, which is indeed remarkable. Surrounded by the Yangtze River and mountains, Nanjing boasts a strategic location that offers both natural beauty and defensive advantages. The city features natural lakes, such as Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake, and hills like Purple Mountain, which is home to historical and cultural sites. This combination of accessibility, natural defenses, and scenic charm likely contributed to Liu Bei's appreciation of Nanjing's geographic position during his negotiations with Sun Quan.
Krispy Kreme, the international doughnut chain, has its headquarters in Winston-Salem, North Carolina.

The "Jacquerie" was a popular uprising that occurred in France during the 14th century. This revolt was a response to the economic and social issues that arose due to the Black Death, a pandemic that swept through Europe between 1347 and 1350, resulting in the death of approximately one-third of the population. The plague led to a significant decrease in the labor force, causing wages to rise and putting pressure on agricultural income due to lower rents and food demand.

In France, these economic challenges, combined with existing social tensions, led to the Jacquerie uprising. The movement was characterized by widespread resistance from peasants and urban workers who demanded greater earnings and better living conditions. The Jacquerie, along with other European uprisings such as the Peasants' Revolt in England and revolts in Italian and Flemish cities, marked a significant period of social unrest during the mid-14th century.

Kanye West finished recording his first album, "The College Dropout," in Los Angeles. This was after he had crafted much of the album's production in less than fifteen minutes at a time, using his Louis Vuitton backpack filled with old disks and demos. Despite the album being leaked months before its release date, West used this opportunity to review and refine it. He added string arrangements, gospel choirs, improved drum programming, and new verses. West's perfectionism led to the postponement of the album's release date three times from its initial date in August 2003.

The term for the close proximity and ending of life of an organism, typically through feeding, is referred to as "true predation." This concept is used in ecology to classify predators based on their feeding patterns and the nature of their interaction with prey species. True predation is distinct in that it results in the death of the prey organism.

Hydrogen's electron and proton are not bound together in the plasma state. This is because, in a plasma, hydrogen is ionized, resulting in high electrical conductivity, high emissivity, and sensitivity to magnetic and electric fields. The Sun and other stars emit light due to the high emissivity of hydrogen plasma. In the solar wind, hydrogen plasma interacts with the Earth's magnetosphere, creating Birkeland currents and the aurora.

The city's architecture primarily features the Georgian style, as seen in many of its buildings. Although there are also modern landmark structures, such as the County Hall tower and The Elysian, the Georgian style remains a dominant feature of the city's architectural landscape.

Raphael is depicted in St. Peter's by a mosaic replica of his famous final work, the Transfiguration. The mosaics in St. Peter's, including Raphael's, showcase lively Baroque compositions and are based on designs or canvases from various artists such as Ciro Ferri, Guido Reni, Domenichino, and Carlo Maratta. The creation of these mosaics was a collaborative effort involving artists like Giovanni Battista Calandra, Fabio Cristofari, and Pietro Paolo Cristofari in the 17th and 18th centuries. These mosaics also served as papal gifts on occasion.

The Japanese refer to the atomic bombings and the Soviet invasion as the "Twin Shocks." This term reflects the profound impact of these events on Japan, which ultimately led to the country's surrender and the end of World War II. On August 10, the Japanese Cabinet made the "sacred decision" to accept the Potsdam Declaration under the condition that the Emperor's sovereign status be preserved. Following the American government's ambiguous reply regarding the emperor's authority, the Emperor broadcast the rescript of surrender on August 15, marking the end of the war.

The expansion of cotton and agriculture in the Uzbek SSR during the period between 1927 and 1934 was mainly concentrated in the southern region. This was a time of significant change in the agricultural landscape of the region, with the implementation of Soviet collectivization policy leading to the collectivization of agriculture and a rapid expansion of cotton production. The shift towards collective farming and cotton production was particularly pronounced in the southern areas, which became a focus for these agricultural developments.

Abdel Fattah el-Sisi was elected as the President of Egypt in the 2014 presidential election, which took place on May 26-28 of that year. El-Sisi, who was the head of the Egyptian Armed Forces at the time, resigned from the military to run for office. He won the election in a landslide, but the victory was marred by a low voter turnout of 46% and a boycott of the election by the Muslim Brotherhood and some liberal and secular activist groups. El-Sisi was sworn into office on June 8, 2014.

The Constantinian basilicas were constructed in the 4th century. This information comes from the context of a discussion about the history of religious architecture, where it is mentioned that these basilicas were among the few large stone buildings constructed during that time period, with many smaller buildings being built during the 6th and 7th centuries. The Carolingian Empire later revived the basilica form of architecture in the 8th century. The Constantinian basilicas are known for their use of a transept, which forms the "arms" of a cross-shaped building that are perpendicular to the long nave. Other new features of religious architecture that emerged during this time include the crossing tower and a monumental entrance to the church, usually located at the west end of the building.

Josip Broz Tito, the leader of Yugoslavia from 1943 until his death, passed away in 1980. Tito, who was born on May 7, 1892, was a key figure in World War II as the leader of the Partisans, a highly effective resistance movement in occupied Europe. Although his presidency has been criticized for being authoritarian, he was widely regarded as a benevolent dictator due to his economic and diplomatic policies. Tito's internal policies helped maintain peaceful coexistence among the nations of the Yugoslav federation, and he gained international attention as the chief leader of the Non-Aligned Movement, working alongside other prominent global figures such as Jawaharlal Nehru, Gamal Abdel Nasser, and Sukarno.

The official name of the country where Portuguese, a Romance language that originated in what is now Galicia and Northern Portugal, is spoken, is Portugal. This language, which is the common tongue of the Portuguese people, originated from Galician-Portuguese and has a high lexical similarity of 89% with Spanish.

The world's first commercial broadcast automation audio compression system, named Audicom, was launched in 1987. This system was developed by Oscar Bonello, an engineering professor at the University of Buenos Aires, based on the psychoacoustic principle of masking of critical bands and utilizing the capabilities of the IBM PC computer. By the early 2000s, nearly all radio stations around the world had adopted similar technology for their operations.

Ducks Unlimited and the Delta Waterfowl Foundation are examples of groups that represent specific hunting interests, with a focus on waterfowl conservation. These organizations are part of a long-standing tradition of hunters who view themselves as conservationists and sportsmen, tracing back to the influence of Theodore Roosevelt and the Boone and Crockett Club. In addition to promoting hunter education and protecting hunting opportunities for future generations, these groups often engage in advocacy efforts directed at federal and state governments.

The 7-inch Extended-Play (EP) format could hold recordings with durations ranging from 10 to 15 minutes. This was achieved by attenuating and compressing the sound to reduce the width required by the groove, as these records typically contained one item per side. EP discs were often used to release tracks that were not available on singles, including those from LP albums, in a more cost-effective format for those who owned only 45 rpm players.

Comcast completed the acquisition of the remaining 49% stake in NBCUniversal from General Electric on March 19, 2013. This purchase came more than two years after Comcast initially bought a controlling 51% stake in NBCUniversal in January 2011, following approval by the FCC in December 2010.

New York Alki was established in April 1853, founded by Charles Terry and John Low who remained at the original landing location of the Denny Party at the future site of present-day West Seattle. The name "New York Alki" was derived from a Chinook word meaning "by and by" or "someday," indicating a future promise. For a few years, New York Alki and Duwamps (later to be known as Seattle) competed for dominance, but eventually, New York Alki was abandoned as its residents moved across the bay to join the rest of the settlers.

The Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) is responsible for building and operating the Delhi Metro system. As a mass rapid transit system, it serves many parts of Delhi and the neighboring cities Faridabad, Gurgaon, Noida, and Ghaziabad, carrying millions of passengers every day. El estilo de Lorrain es considerado uno de los más originales en la pintura de paisaje. Aunque se inspiró en los conceptos ideales del clasicismo francés y las innovaciones paisajísticas de los pintores nórdicos, Lorrain desarrolló un lenguaje renovador que se distingue por su gran sentido lírico de la naturaleza. A diferencia de los pintores holandeses, cuyos paisajes se basaban en principios realistas, los paisajes de Lorrain están profundamente alejados de estos, reflejando un mundo mediterráneo más uniforme, sereno y plácido. Su evolución artística fue uniforme, con claras influencias pero con una fuerte impronta personal.

La fosilización es un proceso físico-químico necesario para que un resto corporal o una señal de un organismo sea considerado un fósil. Este proceso implica transformaciones que pueden afectar la composición y estructura del resto, y depende del tiempo, requiriendo que transcurra un intervalo determinado desde el momento de la producción del resto hasta que se considere fósil. La fosilización es un fenómeno excepcionalmente raro, ya que la mayoría de los componentes de los seres vivos tienden a descomponerse rápidamente después de la muerte.

El FTSE 100 de Londres cerró con un alza del 8,84%, el CAC 40 parisino ascendió en 9,27%, y el DAX de Alemania subió en 5,56%. En Estados Unidos, el Dow Jones, el Nasdaq y el S&P 500 cotizaron con alzas mayores al 3%. Las acciones financieras fueron las más beneficiadas, con algunos bancos, como el asediado HBOB, recuperando cerca del 50%.

Las bolsas asiáticas también recibieron el plan favorablemente, con el Nikkei japonés ascendiendo en un 3,76%, y las subidas más dramáticas en Shanghai y el Hang Seng de Hong Kong, con ganancias del 9,46% y 9,61%, respectivamente. En América Latina, la bolsa de Buenos Aires registró su mayor alza desde 2002, con un ascenso del 10,24%, y el Bovespa brasileño cerró con ganancias de un 7,10%.

A pesar de estas alzas, algunos expertos mostraron escepticismo. John Kyriakopoulos, estratega del National Australia Bank Capital, comentó que las acciones recientes "sólo impidieron que la crisis de financiamiento empeorara, en lugar de revertirla". El plan de rescate fue descrito por el Tesoro de Estados Unidos como un programa de garantía temporal para la industria, con el objetivo de restaurar la confianza en los mercados y las instituciones financieras. El Presidente George W. Bush destacó que este era un momento central para la economía de América.

El término "paleolítico" proviene del griego παλαιός, palaiós, que significa "antiguo", y λίθος, lithos, que significa "piedra". Etimológicamente, "paleolítico" significa "piedra antigua". Fue creado por el arqueólogo John Lubbock en 1865 para contrastarlo con el término "neolítico", que significa "piedra nueva". El Paleolítico es el periodo más largo de la existencia del ser humano, abarcando aproximadamente el 99% de la misma, y se extiende desde hace unos 2,59 millones de años (en África) hasta hace unos 12 000 años. Este periodo, junto con el Mesolítico/Epipaleolítico y el Neolítico, forma parte de la Edad de Piedra, denominada así por la elaboración de utensilios líticos que caracterizan este periodo en contraposición a la posterior Edad de los Metales.

La Saccharomyces cerevisiae se emplea en la investigación del sistema de transporte intracelular. En la década de 1970, Randy W. Schekman comenzó a investigar este sistema utilizando la genética de la levadura Saccharomyces cerevisiae, que es comúnmente utilizada para fabricar pan y cerveza. A través de sus estudios, Schekman observó células de levadura normales y mutadas, identificando que en las células mutadas, las vesículas no entregaban su carga de manera ordenada, sino que se acumulaban en ciertas partes de la célula. Este fenómeno se debía a una causa genética, lo que llevó a Schekman a determinar tres tipos de genes que participan en el sistema de transporte celular.

Los coches de vapor libre no triunfaron en el siglo XX principalmente por dos razones. En segundo lugar, el invento del arranque eléctrico contribuyó a que la idea de los autos de vapor fuera definitivamente descartada. Estos factores, junto con la búsqueda de una fuerza motriz más ligera y flexible, llevaron a que los coches de vapor libre no tuvieran éxito en comparación con los modelos de gasolina que estaban en auge.

Además, se menciona que una combinación de moléculas fuertemente dadoras y aceptoras no garantiza la formación del complejo si ocurre una transferencia total de carga, ya que esto resultaría en especies que se comportan como sustancias iónicas aislantes. En los compuestos orgánicos conductores conocidos, el grado de transferencia de carga es menor de la unidad, generalmente alrededor de 0,5.

Las primeras escuelas en lo que es actualmente Ontario fueron inauguradas durante la década de 1780. Estas escuelas, conocidas como common schools, enseñaban hasta lo que constituye actualmente la educación básica o elemental. Los colores del pavimento en el paseo del arco iris de Oxford St en Taylor Square, Sídney, fueron ordenados a ser eliminados principalmente por razones de seguridad vial. Gaudí se adscribe al modernismo debido a varios factores que se destacan en su obra. En primer lugar, su afán de renovación, que se lleva a cabo sin romper con la tradición, es una característica fundamental del modernismo. Además, su búsqueda de la modernidad y el sentido ornamental aplicado a sus obras son aspectos que lo vinculan con esta corriente. Gaudí también otorga un carácter multidisciplinar a sus realizaciones, donde los trabajos artesanales juegan un papel fundamental. Aunque añade ciertas dosis de barroquismo y mantiene lenguajes arquitectónicos tradicionales, su obra se caracteriza por la inclusión de adelantos tecnológicos y la inspiración en la naturaleza, lo que le otorga un toque de originalidad. Estos elementos combinados proporcionan a su obra un sello personal y único en la historia de la arquitectura, consolidando su adscripción al modernismo.

La propuesta del general estadounidense David Petraeus plantea la retirada de 30,000 tropas estadounidenses de Iraq para julio de 2008, reduciendo el número de tropas a la cantidad original de más de 130,000. Esta propuesta fue parte de un plan que buscaba una presencia estadounidense prolongada en Iraq, al menos durante diez años, según la declaración de Nancy Pelosi. Aunque el plan fue apoyado por el Embajador para Bagdad Ryan Crocker, enfrentó críticas tanto de demócratas como de republicanos. Los demócratas, como Barak Obama y Joseph Biden, criticaron la guerra y la presencia de tropas, mientras que algunos republicanos, incluido Chuck Hagel, expresaron escepticismo sobre el logro de un acuerdo político en Iraq y sugirieron que era hora de retirar no solo los refuerzos, sino también las tropas originales. El presidente George W. Bush, que había ordenado un aumento de 30,000 tropas para alcanzar objetivos militares y garantizar la paz, se esperaba que discutiera y posiblemente condicionara el plan de Petraeus en una conferencia televisiva. Petraeus reconoció que la reconciliación en Iraq aún no se había logrado, aunque se estaban dando pasos en esa dirección.

En Tailandia, el Ejército llevó a cabo un golpe de Estado el 22 de mayo de 2014, dos días después de declarar ley marcial. El jefe de las fuerzas armadas, Prayuth Chan-ocha, anunció el golpe en un mensaje televisado, argumentando que buscaban impedir la muerte de más personas y la escalada del conflicto entre detractores y simpatizantes del Gobierno tras más de ocho meses de protestas casi diarias. El golpe ocurrió después de que fracasara una reunión promovida por los generales para forzar un acuerdo entre las facciones políticas enfrentadas. Con el golpe, los militares buscaron "reformar la estructura política, la economía y la sociedad". Además, se tomaron medidas como la suspensión de los derechos constitucionales, la declaración de toque de queda, el cese de la programación de radio y televisión, la prohibición de asambleas públicas y la ampliación de la censura a medios internacionales.

La OMPI, o Organización Mundial de la Propiedad Intelectual, es un organismo de las Naciones Unidas que se dedica a la promoción y protección de la propiedad intelectual a nivel mundial. Se conmemora el Día Mundial de la Propiedad Intelectual el 26 de abril, fecha en la que se creó la OMPI. La organización celebra este día anualmente con el objetivo de concienciar al público sobre la importancia de respetar las licencias comerciales y de entender que descargar material pirata de Internet es un delito. La OMPI también busca crear conciencia sobre el impacto de la piratería en las industrias protegidas por el derecho de autor y su contribución al crecimiento económico. Además, la OMPI aborda el impacto de las leyes de propiedad intelectual en proyectos libres, como Wikipedia, y promueve el conocimiento sobre herramientas de propiedad intelectual en el desarrollo de las artes, culturas, empresas y tecnología.

La escala Fujita mejorada (EF) se desarrolló como una mejora de la vieja escala Fujita para clasificar tornados basándose en el daño causado. Esta mejora incluyó el uso de estimaciones de vientos más precisas y una mejor descripción del daño. A pesar de estos cambios, la escala EF fue diseñada para que un tornado clasificado según la escala Fujita original recibiera el mismo rango numérico. La escala EF fue implementada en los Estados Unidos a partir de 2007. Además, se utilizan datos de radar de impulsos Doppler, fotogrametría y patrones en el suelo, como marcas cicloidales, para determinar la intensidad y otorgar un rango en la escala EF.

La mayoría de los piratas rechazaban la heterosexualidad, incluso cuando tenían la oportunidad de tener contactos sexuales con mujeres en los puertos, que generalmente eran prostitutas. En su lugar, la homosexualidad y las prácticas homosexuales eran ampliamente aceptadas y parte de la vida diaria en el mundo de los bucaneros o piratas. Las mujeres capturadas rara vez eran utilizadas sexualmente, sino más bien eran usadas para pedir rescate. En su lugar, algunos piratas preferían a los muchachos jóvenes, raptándolos y obligándolos a aprender sobre marinería bajo la tutela de un pirata. Estos lazos podían ser muy fuertes, llegando a dormir y comer juntos, e incluso compartir el botín. Además, los piratas conformaron los primeros "matrimonios" o uniones homosexuales de la historia moderna a través de la institución conocida como matelotage, que era una unión contractual entre dos hombres que incluía la herencia de los bienes en caso de fallecimiento de uno de los "cónyuges".

Las empresas que se listaron inicialmente son Corporación IB-Mei, Indra, Zeltia, Abengoa, Amadeus, Amper, Befesa, Radiotrónica, TPI y Terra. Este proyecto fue oficialmente iniciado a finales de 1999 por una orden del Ministerio español de Economía y posteriormente desarrollado por la Comisión Nacional del Mercado de Valores (CNMV). Las empresas que cotizan en el Nuevo Mercado están sujetas a mayores obligaciones de transparencia en comparación con las que operan en la bolsa española. Es importante destacar que Sogecable, una compañía candidata, no estuvo presente en el estreno debido a que no cumplió con los requisitos necesarios para su incorporación.

La definición primitiva de ciertas palabras en el latín vulgar cambió debido al contagio del contexto semántico habitual, entre otras causas. Este cambio se debió a la evolución del lenguaje y a cómo las palabras se adaptaron a nuevos contextos y usos. Por ejemplo, el término clásico "equus" que significaba "caballo" fue reemplazado por "caballus", que se refería a un "caballo de carga, rocín". Este cambio refleja cómo las palabras pueden evolucionar en significado a medida que se integran en el uso cotidiano y se ven influenciadas por el contexto en el que se utilizan.

Los objetos transneptunianos (TNOs) son cuerpos celestes que orbitan el Sol más allá de Neptuno. Después del descubrimiento de Plutón y Caronte, no se encontraron más TNOs hasta el descubrimiento de (15760) 1992 QB1 en 1992. Desde entonces, se han observado cientos de estos objetos. La mayoría de los TNOs son reconocidos como parte del cinturón de Kuiper, que es un enjambre de cuerpos helados que son sobrantes de la formación del sistema solar y que orbitan cerca del plano de la eclíptica más allá de Neptuno. Aunque ninguno de estos objetos es tan grande como Plutón, algunos, como Sedna, fueron inicialmente descritos en los medios de comunicación como «nuevos planetas».

La eliminación del cañón del avión Typhoon implicaba varios cambios. Aunque el cañón no se consideraba inadecuado, se percibía como innecesario debido a que el armamento con misiles era más adecuado para el rol de caza del Typhoon. Sin embargo, la eliminación del cañón afectaría a las características de vuelo del avión, lo que requeriría modificaciones en el software de vuelo. Estas modificaciones tendrían que ser costeadas por la RAF. A pesar de esto, la RAF decidió que todos sus Typhoon llevarían el cañón, aunque no sería utilizado, con el objetivo de ahorrar dinero al reducir el coste de los requerimientos para los equipos de tierra y evitar los efectos de fatiga al disparar el cañón. La RAF mantuvo la opción de activar los cañones en un tiempo mínimo si los requerimientos operacionales variaran.

El mayor colectivo beneficiado por el indulto masivo aprobado ayer son los insumisos, es decir, los objetores de conciencia que se negaron a realizar cualquier tipo de prestación social sustitutoria del servicio militar. De estos, 30 estaban condenados a penas de cárcel, pero "casi ninguno" de ellos se encontraba en prisión en ese momento. Los 430 restantes estaban condenados a inhabilitación para desempeñar trabajos en la Administración, recibir becas, subvenciones y firmar contratos con organismos oficiales. Estas prohibiciones serán extinguidas para ellos. Además, los que estaban inhabilitados por 10 años, según el Código Penal anterior a 1998, verán rebajada su pena a cuatro años, lo que significa que ya la habrán cumplido. A los condenados hasta cuatro años a partir de 1994 se les ha aplicado el indulto total.
